title: Divers Find What May Be the World’s Oldest Shipwreck
paragraphs: Pottery, as one archaeologist puts it, never really goes away: it merely breaks into ever smaller pieces. That durability may explain how a cargo of storage jars has outlasted the ship that carried it by some 4,500 years, in shallow water off Kekova, west of Antalya. Its discoverers believe the wreck is the oldest yet found, edging past the roughly 4,200-year-old wreck off Dokos in Greece by about three centuries.

Associate Professor Hakan Öniz of Akdeniz University found the site in 2024 on the strength of local seafarers’ hints. The hull has rotted away entirely; what remains is a spread of large jars, many with a raised clay belt, lodged in a rocky slope, which divers spent roughly four months extracting from encrusting barnacles. A tentative reading of the clay places some of the jars, or their raw material, in the Central Jordan Valley. For Karin Sowada of Macquarie University, the find is “a time capsule of ancient trade.”

That said, the headline claim deserves scepticism until it has weathered review. The work has yet to be peer reviewed, the proposed date of about 2700–2400 BCE is provisional, with earlier or later dates not excluded, and analysis of the residue, which could be olive oil, wine or tree resin, is incomplete. Of the voyage itself nothing is known beyond the authors’ conjecture that the ship was riding out a storm when the rocks claimed it.

questions.q: Why does the writer say pottery outlasts ships?
questions.a: Pottery never disappears; it only breaks into smaller pieces.

questions.q: What do the authors say about how the ship was lost?
questions.a: They suggest it was sheltering from a storm when it hit the rocks.

questions.q: Why should the headline claim be treated sceptically?
questions.a: It is not yet peer reviewed and the date is provisional.
